title: Pediatrics Outpatient Experience for EPAC Cohort Students
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The 1-2 year curriculum partners students and core clinical faculty for the longitudinal development of clinical skills in a mentored learning environment. Each students is assigned to a learning community with 1-2 core faculty members. Students will work within their learning communities to gain the core foundational clinical method knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviors necessary to provide optimal patient care in a dynamic healthcare environment. Half of the student's clinics will be conducted in an academic general pediatrics clinic. For the other half, students will be given an opportunity to explore a pediatric sub-specialty or community pediatrics clinic.

title: Peds Continuity Clinic
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The Pediatric Continuity Clinic course is an optional elective course for students in the Pediatric section on the Primary Care Track. The primary goal is to prepare the student for their upcoming ambulatory continuity clinic experience during their residency.

title: Peds Experience in International Health Care: Peru
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Twelve day rotation in several sites in Peru observing and participating in the developmental evolution of medical and public health care.  The student will confront the challenges and value of preventive health and general public health and hygiene instruction.  The integration of efforts to change or improve health care provision for individuals or communities within the economics, the belief system, and the political context will be a focus within an ecological approach.

title: Peer Advising
description: Practicum in peer advising and mentoring. Serve as Peer Advisor for the Communication major under the direction of the Undergraduate Academic Advisor. Serve as Student Advisory Committee. Instructor consent required. May be taken three times for credit.

title: Peer Attending UUSOD Clinic
description: Students will explore the foundations of evaluating clinical treatment, directing clinical treatment, and giving effective and meaningful feedback. Working with an assigned attending, students will supervise a lower classman in three of the following: a simple restorative, fixed prosthodontic, removable prosthodontic, periodontal or diagnosis procedure. Student will perform the usual duties of an attending dentist and will evaluate their assigned student’s work and give constructive feedback.

title: Peer Mentoring I
description: This is a 1-credit training course for peer mentors in the University Counseling Center’s (UCC) Mindfulness Center. In order to register for the course, students must have applied and been accepted to the UCC’s Resilient U mentoring program. In Fall semesters, mentors learn about the history and practice of mindfulness in relation to psychological resilience and social justice. They develop skills to teach others mindfulness through both the Mindfulness Center’s workshops, and through designing their own projects to share with the university community. Students who wish to repeat the course for credit will be considered Advanced Students and a syllabus will be designed specifically for each individual.

title: Peer Mentoring II
description: This is a 1-credit training course for peer mentors in the University Counseling Center’s (UCC) Mindfulness Center. In order to register for the course, students must have completed the Fall semester course (ED PS 3810). In Spring semesters, mentors build on the mindfulness, basic helping skills, and crisis response training introduced in Fall semester. Course content will target specific groups identified by student interest, move to more advanced facilitation training, and continue examination of social positions in context. Mentors will continue to design projects to share with the university community. Students who wish to repeat the course for credit will be considered Advanced Students and a syllabus will be designed specifically for each individual.

title: Peer Tutoring
description: Students will enhance their understanding of concepts and issues in ESS by tutoring students in ESS courses and attending peer tutoring seminars.

title: Peer Tutoring in Nutrition and Integrative Physiology
description: Students will enhance their understanding of concepts and issues in NUIP by tutoring students in NUIP courses and attending peer tutoring seminars.

title: People & Place: Experiences in Community Development
description: Meets with URBPL 3101.  People & Place is a two semester introduction to architecture and urban planning, co-taught by members of the architecture and planning faculty.  The courses weave together the two disciplines through the use of the humanities and the social sciences.  In addition to attending lectures on a variety of urban-based theories, students will also work on a series of community development projects directed by practicing architects, planners, and other community professionals.  The objective is to make direct field applications of theories and methods important to a variety of community based disciplines.  The course is open to all students with a cumulative 3.4 GPA or better.

title: People & Place: Experiences in Community Development
description: People & Place is a two semester introduction to architecture and urban planning, co-taught by members of the architecture and planning faculty.  The courses weave together the two disciplines through the use of the humanities and the social sciences.  In addition to attending lectures on a variety of urban-based theories, students will also work on a series of community development projects directed by practicing architects, planners, and other community professionals.  The objective is to make direct field applications of theories and methods important to a variety of community based disciplines.  The course is open to all students with a cumulative 3.4 GPA or better.

title: People and Nature, Past and Future
description: Are people part of nature? In this course we will explore a variety of approaches taken by scientists and other experts to this question. Through the close reading of peer-reviewed articles, students will learn to articulate the scientific processes and philosophies that inform our understanding of the human relationship with the non-human world and deconstruct concepts that imply a separation between humans and nature. We’ll explore topics in ecology, conservation biology, anthropology, ecosystem services, environmental justice, complex systems, and more. Students will gain conceptual tools that will allow them to critically examine how perspectives on the human-nature relationship inform policy- and decision-making processes within governments, NGOs and the private sector. By linking social and ecological systems, we’ll build an interdisciplinary framework for imagining the future of humanity as ecological citizens.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Europe
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Within the last two decades, Europe has seen the end of the Cold War, civil wars, the rise of new nation-states, and an enlargement of the European Union, all of which resulted in large movements of people across national boundaries as well as across the borders of Europe. Taking an anthropological perspective informed by history, this course examines how political, economic, and cultural processes have impacted the lives of the people in contemporary Europe.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Europe
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Within the last two decades Europe has seen the end of the Cold War, civil wars, the rise of new nation-states, and an enlargement of the European Union, all of which resulted in large movements of people across national boundaries as well as across the borders of Europe. Taking an anthropological perspective informed by history, this course examines how political, economic, and cultural processes have impacted the lives of the people in contemporary Europe.

title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: This course is an introduction to the peoples and cultures of Latin America. It begins with an overview of the cultural geography of Latin America and the people of this region. The course examines how European and African contact and the mixing of cultural, economic, and political values have shaped this geographic space. Current Latin American issues are presented in a historical context. A major theme throughout the course is that anthropological methods and theory can be used to frame and solve contemporary Latin American issues.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the Middle East
description: The turmoil of Middle Eastern life has its roots in ideas and lifestyles developed over thousands of years. This course examines the land and people, analyzing the role of ethnicity, religion, politics, economics, and values in every day behavior.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the Middle East
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Meets with MID E 3713. Additional work required of graduate students.  See MID E 3713 for course description.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the Middle East
description: Meets with MID E 3713. Additional work required of graduate students.  See MID E 3713 for course description.

title: Peoples of the Pacific
college: CT - Sch for Cultural & Social Tran
description: Theories of settlement, distinctive features of island cultures, social and political organization and stratification, and integrative mechanisms such as trading, feasting, warfare, and marriage alliance.

title: Peoples of the Pacific
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Theories of settlement, distinctive features of island cultures, social and political organization and stratification, and integrative mechanisms such as trading, feasting, warfare, and marriage alliance.

title: Peoples of the Pacific
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Additional work required of graduate students. Peoples of the Pacific covers the archaeological history of the Pacific including theories of settlement and the distinctive features of island cultures. In addition, the class will cover the social and political organization and stratification of the islands, and the mechanisms behind cultural change among today’s Pacific Islanders including migration, transnationalism, and colonial history.

title: Peoples of Utah
college: CT - Sch for Cultural & Social Tran
description: Studies Mormon and non-Mormon ethnic groups and their contribution to Utah's development. History and culture including folklore and literature of 14 major and several smaller ethnic groups.

title: Peopling of the Planet
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: How did humans come to occupy continents and islands across the planet? This course surveys the story of one of the worlds most successful colonizers: Homo Sapiens. Lectures detail how humans emerged as a species, left Africa to populate Europe, Asia, Australia, eventually reaching the New World and the Pacific Islands. Material focuses on archaeological data sets, methodologies, theories, and debates to investigate the timing, cause and effects of these colonization events. Special attention is given to the relationships between human subsistence, population dynamics and impacts on previously unoccupied lands.

title: Per-Jurisprudenc
college: LW - S.J. Quinney College of Law
description: TITLES VARY, (PER-)

title: Percussion Instrument Study
description: Performance and pedagogy skills for percussion instruments.

title: Percussion Instrument Study--Lab
description: Ensemble participation on secondary instruments or voice.

title: Percussion Pedagogy
description: Resources, techniques, methodologies, and literature for teaching percussion instruments in all levels of development.

title: Perfecting Your Internship/Job Search
description: Staff from Career Services and the Counseling Center collaborate to offer this half-semester, credit/no credit course. Students explore the foundational skills necessary for an effective job search, including researching employers, developing professional connections, creating resumes and cover letters, and interviewing. The class is individualized to student needs through the assignments and individual appointments with career counselors.

title: Performance and Critique Workshop
description: This is a Performance workshop all Musical Theater Majors are required to register for a different levels each semester. THEA 3653 is the spring section of the Sophomore level of the course. It is the fourth in a series of 8 workshops in which all practical/craft classes will perform their current work each week for their departmental colleagues. Performance practice will have a greater role in the Sophomore level of this course. The understanding and practice of giving constructive feedback will remain a substantial weigh. this course may be taken only one time for Credit.

title: Performance and Critique Workshop
description: This is a performance workshop all Musical Theater Majors are required to register at different levels each semester. THEA 2653 is the spring section of the Freshman level of the course. It is the second in a series of 8 workshops in which all practical/craft classes will perform their current work each week for their program colleagues. In the 2nd semester students will begin to perform in weekly sessions and will continue to practice giving constructive feedback. This course may be taken only one time for credit.

title: Performance and Culture
description: Historical and ethnographic study of performance genres and practices as enactments of cultural identity and as sites of cultural struggle, resistance, and transformation. Topics covered include performance as cultural process, performance as a way of knowing, and performance as power.

title: Performance Credit Apprenticeship: Professional Company
description: Performance of repertoire for members of a professional company. Apprenticeship experience is individually approved and overseen by a member of the faculty.

title: Performance Credit: Ballet Ensemble
description: Student participation in productions for ballet majors, choreographed by faculty and guest choreographers.

title: Performance Credit: Ballet Ensemble
description: Credit for performing in Ballet Ensemble.

title: Performance Credit: Ballet Showcase
description: Student participation in productions for Ballet Showcase I, Ballet Showcase II, and other performances approved by faculty.

title: Performance Credit: Ballet West
description: Performance of repertoire for Trainees of Ballet West.

title: Performance Credit: Character Dance Ensemble
description: Meets with BALLE 4610.  Character dance performance for graduate students.

title: Performance Credit: Graduate
description: Credit for performing in Utah Ballet or other approved professional level productions.

title: Performance Credit: Professional
description: Performance credit for performances with a professional company. Professional performance credits must be approved by the School of Dance and overseen by a member of the faculty.

title: Performance Credit: Utah Ballet
description: This course is designed to offer students the opportunity to work with professional choreographers/restagers – both faculty members and guest artists. The process culminates with multiple performances of the choreographic works the students have learned.

title: Performance Groups I
description: For Theatre Majors and Minors. Closely supervised group projects in performance.

title: Performance Nutrition for Coaches and Athletes
description: This on-line class focuses on the link between nutrition and exercise physiology, as they apply to sport performance and health.  This course will contain the theoretical basis of sport nutrition for optimal performance and health, address issues related to inadequate fueling of athletes and active individuals and how a suboptimal diet may interfere with health and training adaptation.  Further, this class is designed to provide knowledge, tools, and skills for athletes and those working with them to apply sports nutrition principles to a variety of sports and activities.

title: Performance Practice I
description: Study of sources and materials specific to performance practices in music prior to 1750.

title: Performance Practice II
description: This course presents musicological research in Classical and Romantic historical performance practices and traditions from 1750 - 1900 , and explores ways in which these conventions can be applied in contemporary performance through active-based learning class activities and live performance opportunities.

title: Performance Workshop
description: This is a performance workshop all Musical Theater Majors are required to register at different levels each semester. THEA 4653 is the Spring section of the Upper Division level of the course and is the 6th and 8th course in a series of 8 workshops in which all practical/craft classes will perform their current work each week for their departmental colleagues. Performance practice will be the major emphasis of the Upper Division level of this course. The understanding and practice of giving constructive criticism.

title: Performing Arts Design Program Seminar
description: Practice and techniques of theatre design collaboration and communication. Rotating topics include communication and conflict resolution techniques, strategies for effective show preparation, analyzing various ways to achieve a design vision, and organizational tools and applications. Students will also observe, review, and critique theatre design work on departmental and professional productions.

title: Perfusion Anatomy, Physiology, and Surgical Repair
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course will cover an in-depth look at the anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology of the major organ systems of the human body with emphasis on the cardiovascular system. Students will also learn the surgical techniques and systems used to repair and replace different heart and lung abnormalities.

title: Perfusion Lab 1
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course is the first in a three-part laboratory course. This will provide experiences with the Heart Lung machine and all extracorporeal circuit components. This course will also provide experiences with designing and assembling an extracorporeal circuit used for cardiopulmonary bypass.

title: Perfusion Lab 2
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This is the second class in a three-part laboratory course. Students will continue gaining hands-on experiences with setting up and priming the extracorporeal circuit. Students will also start to learn how to manage patients on cardiopulmonary bypass using high-fidelity simulation equipment.

title: Perfusion Lab 3
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course is the third in a three-part laboratory course. This course will continue hands-on experience with setting up and priming the extracorporeal circuit. This course will continue to learn how to manage patients on cardiopulmonary bypass. Students will continue weekly simulations as well as setting up and priming the extracorporeal circuit. This course will also cover other equipment related to perfusion technology. There will also be classes set aside for troubleshooting and correction of the extracorporeal circuit and other related perfusion equipment. This course will also simulate crises that may arise on bypass and how to effectively handle them.

title: Perfusion Pharmacology
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course covers pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, anesthetic agents, anti-arrhythmic pharmacology, inotropic/vasopressor pharmacology, vasodilators, pharmacological treatment of congestive heart failure, antimicrobial agents/antibiotics, anticoagulants, heparin induced thrombocytopenia, antithrombin III deficiency, chemotherapeutic agents, immunosuppressive agents, cancer treatment medications, diabetic agents, and pharmacological measurements and mathematics.

title: Perfusion Science 1
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course will be a broad overview/ introduction to all thing’s pertaining to Cardiovascular perfusion. You will learn the function of the bypass circuit, its components and their purpose. This will also cover normal physiologic values, perfusion math, and how to maintain these values while on CPB.

title: Perfusion Science 1
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course will be a broad overview/ introduction to all thing’s pertaining to Cardiovascular perfusion. You will learn the function of the bypass circuit, its components and their purpose. This will also cover normal physiologic values, perfusion math, and how to maintain these values while on CPB.

title: Perfusion Science 2
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course will be an extension of the materials covered in Perfusion Science 1. We will look at the function of the human body as well as how to maintain normal parameters while on CPB. This course will cover anticoagulation as well as its reversal, blood interactions, and hypothermia on CPB.

title: Perfusion Science 3
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course will be an extension of the materials taught in Perfusion Science 1 and 2. We will discuss transplants, autotransfusion, TEG, ultrafiltration/dialysis, embolic events, alternative approaches to CPB, and the different responses of the body to CPB.

title: Perfusion Standards and Liability Management
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course is designed to help perfusion students understand the standards of the perfusion profession, how to promote quality, what quality in perfusion looks like, the inherent risk of cardiopulmonary bypass, and how to manage liability or risk. Students will develop process improvement plans and will identify potential safety issues that could arise during cardiac surgery. In preparation for hospital rotations, students will identify how they can provide quality perfusion services while seeking to implement skills and practices which will hope to mitigate risk. As a part of discussing quality standards, we will discuss the importance of the cardiac surgery team and its’ members importance in improving the standard of care.

title: Perinatal Genetics
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Provides fundamentals of perinatal genetics for genetic counseling students prior to clinical rotations. Provides overview of topics in perinatal genetics including management of normal and complicated pregnancy, genetic screening, prenatal diagnostic techniques and indications, teratogens and infertility. Covers the diagnosis and management of pregnancies complicated by maternal and fetal genetic disease, fetal anomalies, and pregnancy loss as well as reproductive options such as pregnancy termination. Core and guest lectures are supplemented with interactive discussions and student presentations.

title: Perinatal Medicine
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The goal of this elective is to familiarize the student with the field of perinatal medicine.  The student will gain experience in genetic counseling and diagnosis and antepartum assessment of fetal well-being and maturity.  Outpatient antepartum care of the high-risk pregnant patients including conditions such as Rh sensitization, diabetes mellitus, and hypertensive diseases of pregnancy will be covered.  The student will also gain experience in inpatient management and high-risk patients, both in Labor and Delivery and on the inpatient ward.  The student will be required to select and present one patient weekly to the perinatal division.

title: Period Hair Styles
description: Examines the history of hairstyle and its practical application for theatrical performance. Research techniques, period silhouette, and setting patterns will be explored. Script analysis toward the purpose of choosing appropriate hairstyles for each character will be the main focus of required lab work.

title: Periodontics I (Periodontal Anatomy & Science)
description: This course is designed to introduce and reinforce the foundational and basic science knowledge that is necessary to provide periodontal patient care. Clinical application of information is emphasized in the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning of patient periodontal care.

title: Periodontics I Clinic
description: Clinical applications of Non-surgical periodontal therapy.

title: Periodontics II (Non-Surgical)
description: This course is designed to provide the learner with information regarding the surgical aspects of the treatment of periodontal disease, as well as the systemic conditions which may affect periodontal surgery. Current trends in periodontics will be emphasized and the relationships between the dental hygienist, general practitioner, and the periodontal specialist will be underscored in the context of the role of all health care providers in the management of periodontal disease.

title: Periodontics II Lab  (Non-Surgical)
description: This course will introduce the student to the principles and techniques of periodontal data collection, instrumentation and debridement via a series of lectures, demonstrations and skill-building exercises in the simulation lab and clinic. Students will learn how to accurately assess and record periodontal clinical findings, and perform supra and subgingival bacterial plaque biofilm and calculus removal essential to successful phase 1, nonsurgical periodontal therapy. This course builds on the foundational knowledge presented in Periodontics I (7129) and Periodontics II (7155.) Critical thinking and decision-making skills are applied in determining diagnosis, prognosis, treatment planning and non-surgical periodontal instrumentation as an integral component of comprehensive dental care. At the end of this course the student should be prepared to perform entry level periodontal patient therapy. .

title: Periodontics III
description: This course is designed to provide the learner with information regarding the surgical aspects o the treatment of periodontal disease, as well as the systemic conditions which may affect periodontal surgery. Current trends in periodontics will be emphasized and the relationships between the dental hygienist, general practitioner, and the periodontal specialist will be underscored in the context of the role of all health care providers in the management of periodontal disease.

title: Periodontics III
description: This course is designed to provide the learner with information regarding the surgical aspects of the treatment of periodontal disease, as well as the systemic conditions which may affect periodontal surgery. Current trends in surgical periodontics will be emphasized and periodontal specialist referral guidelines will be underscored in the context of the management of periodontal disease.

title: Periodontics III
description: This course is designed to provide the learner with information regarding the surgical aspects of the treatment of periodontal disease, as well as the consideration of pertinent systemic conditions, which may affect periodontal surgery. It builds on the foundational knowledge presented in Periodontics I and II. Topics covered in this course will include the rationale, indications and contraindications for various periodontal surgical procedures, including mucogingival surgery, treatment of bony defects, osseous grafting and periodontal tissue regeneration. The mechanisms and timing of healing of surgical sites, as well as post-surgical treatment will be presented. Current trends in surgical periodontics will be emphasized and guidelines for periodontal specialist referral will be underscored in the context of the management of periodontal disease.

title: Permitting and Reclamation
description: The course is a requirement for the mining engineering program. Students and the instructor will explore the concepts mine permitting and reclamation planning. The course will cover: Environmental Movement; History of environmental permitting; Reclamation; Reclamation planning.

title: Persian Conversation
description: This course provides students the opportunity to improve their skills in speaking and listening, to expand their cultural awareness, and to increase their self-confidence in the language. Designed to be taken with 1020, 2010, or 2020, but open to any student not enrolled at the 3000/4000 level. No written work. Credit/Non-Credit grading.

title: Persian Culture and Civilization
description: Study of major events, movements, genres, and trends in Iranian history and Persian literature and culture. Topics include, the Iranian world view and historical memory, survey of Iranian history from ancient times to the present, the development of classical and modern prose and poetry styles, Zoroastrian thought, Iranian archetypes, sufism, Iranian revolutions in the 20th century in the mirror of Persian literature.

title: Person-Centered Teaching
description: Required for nursing students in the Master of Science program with an emphasis on Nursing Education, students engage with community partners to promote equity regarding healthcare education and access.

title: Personal and Interdependent Resiliency
description: Exploration of concepts and skills that lead to personal and interdependent resiliency including couples, families, corporations, and communities. Experientially based for personal application and skill development for self understanding, resilient paradigms, directioning, and adaptation.

title: Personal Financial Planning
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: Through the use of case analysis, this course provides students with an opportunity to learn the principles, theories, and processes relating to personal financial management. While anyone could benefit from the course, it is most suitable for those preparing for a career as a Certified Financial Planner (CFP), a Certified Public Accountant (CPA), an attorney, or individuals planning to advise on the financial affairs of individuals, families and small business owners. Topics include personal balance sheet assessment, understanding and improving cash-flows, debt analysis, budget creation, goal identification, investment analysis, retirement Income forecasting, education funding analysis, insurance planning, the impact of income tax, estate planning, and small business owner issues.

title: Personal Financial Planning
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: Through the use of case analysis, this course provides students with an opportunity to learn the principles, theories and processes relating to personal financial management.  While anyone could benefit from the course, it is most suitable for those preparing for a career as a Certified Financial Planner (CFP), a Certified Public Accountant (CPA), an attorney or individuals planning to advise on the financial affairs of individuals, families and small business owners. Topics include personal balance sheet assessment, understanding and improving cash-flows, debt analysis, budget creation, goal identification, investment analysis, retirement Income forecasting, education funding analysis, insurance planning, the impact of income tax, estate planning and small business owner issues. This course satisfies the CFP Board’s Personal Financial Planning Capstone Requirement.

title: Personal Selling
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This course provides a comprehensive treatment of the significant accumulated knowledge about selling. The basic objectives, concepts, and tools required to be an effective salesperson are covered. Laboratories are scheduled to provide detailed feedback on sales presentations and performance so that students can maximize their improvement. consult the current class schedule for information on the special laboratory fee.

title: Personality
description: Comprehensive and systematic analysis of major personality theories. Emphasis on relevance to counseling, teaching, and other applied settings.

title: Personality and Substance Use Disorders
description: Focuses on developmental underpinnings of personality disorders, substance abuse, and other disorders of control. Interplay of substance abuse and disorders of mental health explored from a multitheoretical perspective. Emphasis placed on current research and clinical literature aimed at promoting comprehensive assessment and intervention.

title: Personality Assessment
description: Development, interpretation, and use of the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory. Profile analysis, inference formulation, and report writing. Integration of test data with history and mental status examination and the interventions process.

title: Personality Theories
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Work of the major personality theorists with emphasis on supporting research.

title: Personality Theory and Research
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Graduate students should register for PSYCH 6450 and they will be held to a higher standard or do additional work. Major traditional theoretical approaches to personality and recent theoretical developments. Critical evaluation of theories in terms of personality development and structure. Application of theories to specific domains of behavior.

college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The Personalized Health Care Capstone project is a requirement for the Certificate in Personalized Health Care. For further information, contact the instructor.

title: Personnel Administration in Education
description: Introduction to policy and practice associated with personnel administration in education, including human-resource planning, job analysis and design, recruitment and selection, employee evaluation, compensation, and collective bargaining.

title: Personnel Economics
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This course is an application of economics to human resource management, with particular emphasis on personnel economics. Topics include wages and incentives, hiring, training and human capital, layoffs and turnover, tournaments, efficiency wages, performance measurement, non-wage benefits. Course sessions will consist of a mix of lecture and discussion. Readings will rely heavily on current news articles to illuminate the direct applicability of economics to the current business world. Students will use econometrics skills to analyze data directly relevant to managerial decision-making in HR.

title: Personnel Economics: Managerial Frameworks and Data Analysis
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: Personnel Economics is the application of economic analysis to human resource management questions. Important topics in personnel economics include hiring, incentives, training and skill development, retention, termination, promotions, and careers. Recently, the advent of "big data'" has sparked interest in making data-driven decisions regarding human resource management questions. Analytical methods are now available to allow firms to optimize hiring processes, assess the efficacy of training and skill development initiatives, predict turnover, and test the impact of promotion-based incentives. In this course, data and analysis are complemented by economic frameworks that can be used to interpret the results. Course sessions will mix a variety of learning modes, including: Lecture/discussion where economic and econometric frameworks will be presented, Case studies in which economic frameworks will be applied to real managerial situations, Data analysis lab sessions in which we will write code to analyze data for managerial decision-making.

title: Perspective
college: LW - S.J. Quinney College of Law
description: An introduction to American legal history by identifying some of the main social, political, and economic values used by our legal order to exploit the land mass through the use of the market. This includes different perceptions of the historical past offered by the leading proponents of contrasting views. The primary focus is upon the views of Willard Hurst, however, with most attention given to the 19th century. Satisfies the perspective requirement.

description: Examination of the various types of national, ethnic and folk dances of Europe as they have been adapted to classical ballet performances and other theatrical productions. Additional assignments will be given to graduate students.

title: Perspective on Mathematics
description: Topics from calculus, emphasizing the ideas of calculus rather than the technical aspects.

title: Perspectives in Character Dance
description: Examination of the various types of national, ethnic and folk dances of Europe as they have been adapted to classical ballet performances and other theatrical productions.

title: Perspectives in Comparative Education
description: Examines different perspectives on literacy and literature practice. Course readings, assignments, and discussions focus on what it means to say that literacy is not only the mastery of process that leads to acts of reading and writing, but is also a cultural, social, historical, and political practice. Topic varies. Repeatable for Credit. Students enrolled in 7635 will be expected to meet a higher standard of performance and may be assigned additional work.

title: Perspectives in Comparative Education
description: Examines learning and teaching in formal and informal cultural settings outside the United States. Cross-cultural ethnographic studies will be analyzed from the perspectives of anthropology, sociology and cultural studies. Topic varies. Repeatable for credit.

title: Perspectives in Early Medieval Studies
description: This course traces the emergence of medieval society from the disintegration of the Roman World.

title: Perspectives in Geometry forTeachers
description: Intuitive and computational geometry and trigonometry.

title: Perspectives in Mathematics Teaching and Learning
description: Meets with T L 6722.  Examines school mathematics curriculum and its relationship to contemporary culture.  Course traces relationships among social, political, and mathematics educational policy in 20th-century and U.S. and examines critical analyses of these relationships.  Students enrolled in T L 7722 will be held to a higher standard and may be assigned additional coursework.

title: Perspectives in Mathematics Teaching and Learning
description: Examines school mathematics curriculum and its relationship to contemporary culture. Course traces relationships among social, political, and mathematics educational policy in 20th-century U.S. and examines critical analyses of these relationships.

title: Perspectives in Performance
description: An in-depth evaluation of performance development and aesthetic vision concentrating on various performing groups in Utah from the youth concerts to the professional performing groups.

title: Perspectives in Private Equity
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This course will explore concepts in private equity from the perspective of the general partner, limited partner investors and the underlying fund investment companies. The class will utilize case studies and guest lecturers from industry. The course will seek to explore concepts around partnership structures, legal/deal terms, investor commitment pacing models, private equity's role as an asset class in a well diversified portfolio, manager selection, the current state and trends within Private Equity, basic deal due diligence and private equity strategies for creating value. Students will gain perspectives across Buy Out, Special Situation, Growth Equity and Venture Capital strategies.

title: Perspectives on American Culture
description: An exploration of such questions as: What constitutes quality in America? How is American culture distinctive, and what is progress? These issues and others help students understand significant elements which have shaped the culture and character of the United States.

title: Perspectives on Sport and American Society
description: This course considers both the popular fascination with, and the academic investigation of, sport and American society. Philosophers and sociologists argue that sport has become the one cultural activity that most effectively overcomes distinctions of race, class, gender, ethnicity, politics, and religion, to bind Americans in a community of shared values and aspirations. Conversely, sport has also magnified and reproduced a myriad of social inequalities. Students will routinely appraise how their worldview and personal ethics serve to reproduce, revise, or replace the structure, norms and beliefs associated with local, national, and international sport and physical culture. Through a sociological and historical lens, students will appraise the unifying power of sport, as well as explain how sport serves to reproduce inequalities present in the larger society.

title: Perspectives on Sports and American Society
description: Considers both the popular fascination with and the academic investigation of sports in American society. Some philosophers and sociologists argue that sport has become, if not America's "secular religion," then certainly the one cultural activity that most effectively and pervasively overcomes distinctions of race, class, gender, and ethnicity, as well as politics and religion, to bind Americans in a community of shared values and aspirations. Students gain a deeper understanding of sport in American society and a greater appreciation of the essential unity of learning. Consult semester Class Schedule for the Intellectual Explorations area being offered.

title: Perspectives on Women Artists
description: A survey of women in the visual arts from ancient to modern times. Materials will be presented in slide lectures and in seminar-style discussions.

title: Perspectives on World Health
description: Medical and health issues in the history of selected world cultures and nations.

title: Persuasion and Political Communication
description: Theory and practice in modern persuasion situations, with emphasis on teaching students to become critical consumers of persuasive messages.

title: Persuasion and Social Influence
description: Persuasion and Social Influence surveys theories and concepts related to persuasion and social influence from social and behavioral science approaches. Particular attention will be paid to understanding why and under what conditions individuals’ ideas, attitudes and behaviors are influenced by others. Readings will be drawn from a range of communication areas, including (but not excluding to) science, health, environmental, and risk communication. This course will not presuppose any prior background in quantitative research methods, but will introduce to empirical studies using quantitative research methods.

title: Persuasion Theory and Practices
description: Study and practice of principles of persuasion in public speaking and other forms of communication.

title: Petrogenesis of Igneous and Metamorphic Rocks
description: Mineralogy, chemistry, texture, origin (petrogenesis) and evolution of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Relationships of magmatism and metamorphism to plate tectonics. Roles of magmatism and metamorphism in the evolution of the Earth’s lithosphere, oceans and atmosphere. Two lectures, one lab weekly.

title: Petrography and Petrogenesis
description: Identification of minerals in igneous and metamorphic rocks in flat-stage thin sections by optical means. Textural relations between constituent minerals in rocks and their interpretation. Laboratories consist of studying rock slices in thin section using a petrographic microscope. Two lectures, one lab weekly.

title: Petroleum Field Study
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: The principles of petroleum geology are best illustrated by surface exposures. The same holds for petroleum engineering processes such as pipeline facilities, drilling operations and refining operations. Each students will spend two weeks in the summer in the Central Rocky Mountains and Colorado Plateau region on a field study. The field trips will involve studying cores, outcrops, landforms, and producing field operations. The data and insight from the culminating field site in the Green River Basin of Wyoming will be integrated into the project for CH EN 5171/6156 Reservoir Simulation, which will immediately follow the Field Study.

title: Petroleum Production Engineering
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: This course is a compilation of diverse but essential modules for any practicing petroleum engineer. Included are advanced wireline logging interpretation, artificial life principles, pressure transient analysis principles, basics of safety and risk analysis, petroleum economics, and petroleum resources management systems.

title: Petroleum Production Engineering
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: This course is a compilation of diverse but essential modules for any practicing petroleum engineer. Included are advanced wireline logging interpretation, artificial life principles, pressure transient analysis principles, basics of safety and risk analysis, petroleum economics, and petroleum resources management systems.

title: Petroleum Systems Capstone: PICP 2b
description: This course presents an open-ended petroleum exploration scenario where students must apply the methods and approaches encountered in previous PICP offerings. Industry-standard software will be used in a collaborative, team-based working environment to identify and characterize prospects from an industry dataset. Students will rely on their fundamental knowledge of geology and geophysics to generate prospects and will investigate the impact of (1) hydrocarbon in place estimation methods and other reservoir engineering concepts, (2) risk evaluation, and (3) economics, land issues and legal implications of evaluating petroleum plays and prospects. Offered second half of spring semester.

title: Petroleum Systems Capstone: PICP 3a
description: Meets with GEO 5535. This capstone course provides an opportunity to explore more advanced topics in petroleum geology that were not addressed in the lower level PICP course series in detail. Students will be presented with an open-ended exploration scenario or applied petroleum problem to solve in a team based collaborative manner. This course will draw upon published literature and industry datasets.

title: Petrology
description: For students needing a junior-level general petrology course (e.g., B.S. students in mining engineering). Taught with first half of GEO 3090 Earth Materials II.

title: Petrophysics and  Well Logging
description: Meets with GEO 5260; additional work required of graduate students.  See GEO 5260 for course description.

title: Petrophysics and Well Logging
description: Meets with GEO 6260. Petrophysical links between geophysical and geological variables.  Principles and applications of downhole logging tools. Geophysical, geological, and geological engineering interpretation of logging and other borehole data.

title: PH Seminar - Factors Related to Human Health
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: A series of seminars from faculty and staff from within and outside of the Public Health Program on a variety of topics pertaining to public health. The course is meant for entering doctoral students, as well as MSPH students.The human health seminar (1 credit of the total 3 credit seminar series) focuses on foundational knowledge competencies related to human health. Topic areas include: effects of environmental, biological, genetic, behavioral, psychological factors on population health; social, political, and economic determinants of health; globalization; and One Health.

title: Ph.D Internship IV: District/Agency Administration
description: Supervised experience in administrative educational/community service programs for individuals with disabilities.

title: Ph.D. Capstone Seminar in Integrated Research
description: In this course, students will integrate prior course work and knowledge in the refinement of research questions and conceptual frameworks.  A critical analysis of a substantive and/or intervention area will result in the development of a focused research agenda for the dissertation.  An oral defense of a written final Capstone paper may be part of the Qualifying Examination requirements. The paper is basically the first two chapters of the dissertation: The rationale, importance, and scope of the study (Chapter 1) and the literature review (Chapter 2).

college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: Colloid, interfacial, and electrokinetic theories applied to the design of drug formulations, drug delivery, and therapeutic efficacy.

title: Pharmaceutical Compounding & Drug Delivery Systems
description: Principles and techniques of prescription compounding, record keeping, and patient counseling. This course requires registration for a lab section.

title: Pharmaceutical Economics & Policy
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course explores the interplay between pharmaceutical economics and policy in the US, emphasizing the historical evolution of the health care system and its ongoing transformation. Designed for advanced students, the course provides an in-depth understanding of the economic forces and regulatory frameworks that have shaped the pharmaceutical landscape. The course consists of three modules: (1) The historical foundations of pharmaceutical regulation and financing, (2) the current economic and policy environment, exploring key drivers of pharmaceutical pricing, access, and innovation, and (3) forward-looking analysis, equipping students with the tools to predict the impact of proposed policy changes.

title: Pharmaceutical Policy and Economics
description: This course focuses on pharmaceutical policy and economics, emphasizing the interplay between healthcare systems, pharmaceutical markets, and health outcomes. It includes analysis of the impact of policy decisions on drug pricing, access, and innovation while applying economic principles to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of pharmaceutical interventions.

title: Pharmacodynamics and Pharmacologic Basis of Therapeutics I
description: The pharmacodynamics and pharmacological basis of therapeutics.

title: Pharmacoeconomics
description: Consideration of economic factors affecting the provision and consumption of pharmaceuticals.

title: Pharmacoepidemiology
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Pharmacoepidemiology joins the fields of clinical pharmacology and epidemiology, and it is the study of the use and effects of drugs in large groups of people. Pharmacoepidemiology methods are also used to conduct and evaluate programmatic efforts to improve medication use on a population basis. The aim of the course is to introduce students to the most important issues in pharmacoepidemiology. To this end, the course will emphasize phamacovigilance, surveillance methods, and follow-up studies. The course will present an overview of observational study designs, including drug utilization studies, case reports, and case-control and cohort studies. Description and measurement of drug exposures and outcomes, biases, and confounders as well as their implication in pharmacoepidemiology research will be included. The course contains lectures as well as exercises, and group discussions.

title: Pharmacoepidemiology
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Covers various research methods used in drug development to assess safety and efficacy, with an emphasis on methods other than controlled clinical trials, including analysis of existing databases, population risk trials, and other applications of epidemiologic methods to drug evaluation.

title: Pharmacokinetic Approaches to Drug Delivery
description: Design and analysis of pre-clinical pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies.

title: Pharmacokinetics & Pharmacodynamics
description: Basic principles of in-vivo drug kinetics (linear and non-linear); principles of bioavailability/bioequivalence; physiologic determinates of drug onset and duration; concepts of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion; the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic interface; dosage regimen design; renal and hepatic clearance; using pharmacodynamics to estimate drug half-life and adjust dosages.

title: Philosophy, Theory Development, and Research Methods
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This seminar is designed to give business PhD students an understanding of philosophy of science, theory construction, and empirical tests of theories. The first objective of this seminar is to provide an understanding of philosophy of science. Philosophy of science exposes and questions critical assumptions and methods of science that help us answer some of the most significant questions about scientific knowledge. Like what is knowledge, how is it created, how can it be scrutinized and validated, how does it gain acceptance, why is it always changing. As a creator of scientific knowledge, philosophy of science also nudges students to reflect upon their activities and motivations as a scientist. The second objective of this seminar is to train students in theory construction from idea generation, hypothesis development, to theory development. The discussion will incorporate abstract concepts of theory construction and their application in published research. It is designed to provide students an understanding of how to connect their specific research ideas to different research streams that already exist. After developing theory, the next critical step is its empirical test. The third section of this seminar will focus on analysis methods that can be used to assess how valid is the empirical support for a theory. We will discuss methods such as experimental design, diff-in-diff, regression discontinuity design, power analysis, effect size testing, regression. Theory testing using machine learning methods will also be discussed. Many times such methods are taught across various courses and prevent researchers from seeing how they can be easily used in their research papers.
