The focus of the course will be the influence of resistance training on health, disease, and injury prevention, and the rehabilitation of acute injury and chronic disease and disability.

title: Resort Management
description: Offers a complete approach to the operation of resort properties: historical development, planning, development, investment, financial management, marketing, and future issues and concerns.

title: Resource Conservation and Environmental Management
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: The class approaches resource conservation and environmental management from a geographic perspective and focuses on human-environmental interactions. The course considers the challenges currently facing resource conservationists, the science used to recognize environmental problems, and possible methods to prevent or mitigate the overuse of natural resources. Students in this course study a wide range of topics including food, waste, water, and energy. Expert guest speakers and field trips are incorporated into the class.

title: Resource Management as a Health Professions Education Leader
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course focuses on the effective allocation and management of financial and human resources in a health professions education setting. Financial dynamics specific to academic healthcare settings and budgeting will be emphasized,

title: Responding to Student Writing
description: Theory and practice of responding to graduate writing from all disciplines. Students will be trained to tutor in both in-person and online settings. Student will be hired as a Graduate Writing Fellow for the Graduate Writing Center.

title: Response to Illness across the Lifespan
description: This course focuses on concepts associated with human response to illness across the lifespan.  Emphasis is placed upon evidence based nursing care for patients experiencing illness.  Upon completion, the student will be able to identify and describe evidence-base nursing care that contributes to high quality patient outcomes.

title: Responses to Exile
description: How Jews constructed their own identities and supportive social structures. Jewish law, Jewish ethics, Jewish philosophy, Jewish mysticism, Jewish messiahs and messianism, and Jewish nationalism as tools for survival within the hostile environments of exile.

title: Responsibilities of Business Leaders
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This immersive course surveys the ethical and inclusive leadership skills necessary in our changing global business environment. Delve into topics such as ethical decision-making, sustainable innovation, cultural competency, stakeholder management, employee-wellbeing, and fostering an inclusive work environment. Attendance and participation are core components of this course, as students will engage in real-world case discussions, group simulations, and constructive debates. Students will practice navigating complex ethical dilemmas, understanding and appreciating diverse viewpoints, and strategizing solutions for a wide variety of stakeholders. Develop the skills to become a principled and effective leader of tomorrow.

title: Restorative Technology
description: This is an introductory course in restorative dental technology. Emphasis will be placed on understanding the rationale, advantages and limitations of digital impressions in clinical practice. Students will be introduced to multiple systems in order to compare technologies. Computer Aided Design/Computer Aided Milling (CAD/CAM), along with 3-D Printing and their use in the fabrication of indirect dental restorations and the interrelationship of these technologies with Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) and digitally generated surgical guides for implant placement will also be covered. As a pre-requisite to this course, students must have successfully completed Fixed Prosthodontics I (DENT 7163, 5 credit hours, summer semester), Fixed Prosthodontics II (DENT 7230, 4 credit hours, fall semester) and Fixed Prosthodontics III (DENT 7257, 5 credit hours, spring semester).

title: Retail Real Estate
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This course is designed to provide an overview of key concepts to consider in the development of retail real estate. A historic and analytical review of retail as an asset class, including recent trends in retail real estate, will be discussed to help provide a conceptual framework to consider in planning and executing retail developments in the future. The focus of the course will be on those aspects of the development process that are unique to retail. Consideration will be given to fundamental deal points, due diligence concerns, feasibility issues, and other areas of risk and exposure that are present in retail development. Students completing this course will be better prepared to plan, negotiate, and execute retail developments and be better equipped to identify opportunities in retail real estate going forward.

title: Retirement and Benefits Planning for Families
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: The intent of this course is to provide individuals with knowledge of both retirement plans and employee benefits.  The public retirement plans include Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.  The private plans include defined benefit and defined contribution plans and their regulatory provisions. The specifics of the various plans are analyzed as well as non-qualified deferred compensation plans.  Employee benefits such as health insurance and disability insurance will also be discussed.  Finally, issues that individuals face in retirement such as life-style choices, community choices, and medical issues are discussed.

title: Retirement Planning and Adjustment
description: Information and resources applicable to preretirement preparation and many concerns involved in living through the retirement experience. Economics of aging on both a macro and micro level blending social psychology and group in-class activities so the material is personally applicable for the student and illustrates adjustments that retirees may face.

title: Retirement Planning and Adjustment
description: Information and resources applicable to preretirement preparation and many concerns involved in the retirement experience. Economics of aging on both a macro and micro level blending social psychology and group in-class activities so the material is personally applicable for the student and illustrates adjustments that retirees may face.

title: Review of Intermediate Statistics
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Transition course from undergraduate- to graduate-level statistics.

title: Reviews in Earth Science
description: Review of selected topics encompassing a broad spectrum of disciplines within Earth science. Seminar format emphasizes developing communications skills, teamwork, and collegiality. Required for all students in first year of M.S. programs in Department of Geology and Geophysics. One two-hour meeting weekly.

title: Revising and Editing
description: An advanced course in the practice of writing and revising prose, including reviews of normative grammar and stylistic conventions.

title: Revolutionary Dreams in Soviet Russia
description: Meets with HIST 4230.  Focuses on political, economic, and intellectual debates and conflicts characterizing and shaping Russia in the 1920s.  Examines historical literature and historiography on the period as well as art, architecture, literature, and film.  Explores the creative energy of the revolutionary period to understand why and how relative tolerance in the 1920s gave way to reaction in the 1930s.

title: Revolutionary Dreams in Soviet Russia
description: Meets with HIST 6230.  Focuses on political, economic, and intellectual debates and conflicts characterizing and shaping Russia in the 1920s.  Examines historical literature and historiography on the period as well as art, architecture, literature, and film.  Explores the creative energy of the revolutionary period to understand why and how relative tolerance in the 1920s gave way to reaction in the 1930s.

title: Revolutionary France: 1770-1871
description: Political, social, cultural, and diplomatic history of France from the origins of the French Revolution to the establishment of the third Republic.

title: Rhetoric I: Classical to Early-Modern Rhetoric
description: A survey of rhetorical theories, starting from Greek antiquity and continuing into the early modern period. Readings, assignments, and class discussions trace the developments of classical and medieval rhetorical theories through primary texts and provide familiarity with recent secondary scholarship responding to those developments. Course emphases may vary by instructor/semester.

title: Rhetoric II: Early-Modern to Contemporary Rhetoric
description: A survey of early modern and post-modern rhetorical theories, beginning in the 17th Century and working through to contemporary rhetorical theories. Readings, assignments, and class discussions trace the developments of early-modern to contemporary rhetorical theories through primary texts. Contemporary applications of previous rhetorical theories are also covered. Course emphases may vary by instructor/semester.

title: Rhetoric of Advocacy and Social Change
Rhetoric of Science, Technology, and Medicine
description: This course is designed to furnish students with an in-depth understanding of rhetorical theory and criticism in the context of science, technology, and/or medicine. Students will engage a range of disciplinary and interdisciplinary scholarship that theorizes rhetorical work in this area and models rigorous application of rhetorical tenets and approaches. They will explore subject matters that span scientific fields, technological advancements, and medical protocols and treatments, and they will consider these matters through a variety of diverse lenses related to ethical inquiry, knowledge acquisition, community engagement, and social justice.

title: Rhetoric, Science & Technology Studies
description: This course examines the history of science/technology and its relevance to contemporary society. Employing a rhetorical lens, students study scientific/technological advances, and their related concepts from secularism to globalization. Various genres of scientific written communication are examined for their effectiveness through the ages, with special attention focused on hot topics. This course furthers understanding the relationship among writing, science, and society. Students are strongly advised to take WRTG 2010 or equivalent prior to taking this course.

title: Rhetoric: Aristotle to AI
description: This course provides an overview of many ways that people have engaged in discourse that makes things matter, from ancient Athens to today’s modern society. Although rhetoric was originally concerned with the power of words to help people navigate their differences and make decisions whose outcomes could not be known in advance, today the study of rhetoric considers much more than words, including the power of images, bodies, brands, environments, social movements, politicians, and the whole range of media technologies that organize our lives.

title: Rhetorical and Critical Methods
description: This course takes seriously the idea students are researchers--reading, inquiring into, crafting questions for, and developing tools and strategies to answer questions about the everyday. In it, students will learn about a wide variety of research methods such as close reading, listening, discourse analysis, archival research, translanguaging, and ethnography. These are tools that researchers draw upon to collect, analyze, and make meaning of cultural data. They are also methodologies that are the epistemic and theoretical interests driving the undertaking of research. Ultimately, students in this class will design and pilot a semester-long research study into a cultural phenomenon, both developing researchable questions and selecting appropriate methods to collect data about, interact with, parse, and analyze the rhetorics of everyday life, communities, and/or culture.

title: Rhetorical Criticism
description: Introduction to analysis of public communication (speeches, editorials, advertisements, TV, film, etc.) from a variety of critical perspectives.

title: Rhetorical Styles and Grammars
description: This course focuses on the varieties, characteristics, and function of style in prose writing. Students in this class will cultivate a range of styles by experimenting with and analyzing the effects of such variables as word choice, sentence structure, rhythm, punctuation, grammar, and usage.  We'll observe how style shapes what can be said and to whom, and describe how different styles suit different audiences. We'll also explore how the field of writing studies has theorized about and analyzed style, often from critical perspectives.

title: Rhetorics of Gender
description: This course is designed to give students an introduction to gender research that is distinctly rhetorical. Students will use theories from contemporary and classical rhetoric and criticism to interrogate the construction and performance of gender in a variety of social settings and media, the gendering of the writing studies/writing instruction, and the gendering of the tradition of rhetoric itself.

title: Rheumatology Clinical Clerkship
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Medicine junior clerkship topics: Clinical case study in arthritis.

title: Rhythm, Music and Dance
description: This course reinforces the rhythmic knowledge students will utilize throughout their careers as dancers. The content will explore the fundamentals of rhythmic notation, production, performance, creation of music for dance, and how each of these fundamentals relates to movement.

title: Rifle Marksmanship
description: This class will teach students the safety protocols, shooting skills, and management issues associated with shooting air rifles in state-operated facilities. Students will learn about and practice shooting range protocols, gun safety, range safety, range safety as well as the physical and mental principles of marksmanship. Students will also learn to utilize proper rifle nomenclature in their on-range exercises and competition communications as well as learn to handle .177 Olympic grade, air rifles.

title: Rigging for Games
description: This course is an in-depth study of the art and science of rigging 3D models for animation using industry standard applications. Students will gain an understanding of the concepts and techniques to create custom animation rigs for a variety of characters such as humans, creatures, and inanimate objects. Additional topics include subsets such as the face, clothing, and other components of the character. This is a project-based course in which students design and create functional control interface systems through problem solving and creativity using a variety of core concepts and techniques. Scripting will be employed for the purpose of automating tasks and other procedures.

title: Rise of Global Capitalism
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Graduate students should register for POL S 6750 and will be held to higher standards and/or additional work. Explores the factors and conditions that lead countries to decide whether and how to promote the development of their industries and economies. Emphasis is placed on the similar and different ways political forces influence the structure and process of industrial development in the countries studied.

title: Rise of the Bots: AI and Algorithmic Communication in Society
description: This course considers the role of AI, AR, VR and new bot applications and technologies in communication and the implications they have on and for society. Most communication-based professions are now reliant on web metrics, web analytics, algorithmic data, machine learning, and AI capabilities for messaging, engagement, predictive modeling and beyond. This course offers a rich space to explore the histories, theories and applications of AI, AR, VR and related technologies while considering their future impacts on professions such as journalism, political communication, and marketing which have come to rely on them.

title: Risk and Insurance
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: Topics include the management of personal risks through the use of insurance and non-insurance techniques of risk control. Also included is a survey of personal insurance coverages and social insurance programs.

title: Risk Assessment and Management
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This semester course will review the fundamentals of risk, risk assessment and risk management. This will include the history of risk concepts, assessment approaches and risk management tools. Case studies will include examples of catastrophic failures in risk assessment and management where human safety is concerned. Risk management tools will be reviewed and students will gain practice by applying assessment and management tools to real world industrial settings. Changing societal attitudes and expectations of risk will also be reviewed.

title: Risk Assessment and Management
description: This course will review the fundamentals of risk, risk assessment and risk management. This will include the history of risk concepts, assessment approaches and risk management tools. Case studies will include examples of catastrophic failures in risk assessment and management where human safety is concerned. Risk management tools will be reviewed and students will gain practice by applying assessment and management tools to real world industrial settings. Changing societal attitudes and expectations of risk will also be reviewed.

title: Risk Management
description: Understand the function and use of formal and informal risk management tools. Apply risk management to mine engineering problems and challenges and to safety and health management problems and challenges. Understand the role of risk management in protecting whole organizations, in safety and health management and in S&H management systems. (Completion of MG EN 5350 Health & safety preferred but not required.)

title: Risk Management & Insurance Planning for Families
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: This course provides an introduction to financial planning concepts and in-depth study of risk management concepts, tools, and strategies for individuals and families, such as health, disability, and long-term care insurance; life insurance; property and casualty insurance; liability insurance; and Social Security. Assignments and case studies will provide experience in selecting insurance products suitable for individuals and families. The objectives required from the Board of Standards for the Certified Financial Planner designation will be covered.

title: Rivers & Community
description: This field based course connects rivers to our daily lives in the context of sustainable living. Students participating in this floating classroom will participate in topics surrounding sustainable development and management of river resources, including water, recreation, cultural heritage, and management of rivers as they relate to sustainable community development and management.

title: RNA-sequencing Computational Analysis
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) is an important technology that can be used to understand cellular states. This course provides an introduction to technologies and tools used to interpret RNA-seq data, including analysis of RNA-seq in bulk, single-cell, and spatial analyses. Throughout the course, students will engage in hands-on activities, practical exercises, and assignments to enable them to reinforce their understanding and prepare them to confidently analyze their own RNA-seq data. Students are expected to have a working knowledge of R, python, and basic genomics, as well as familiarity with the Linux command line.

title: Roadside MBA: The Economics of Growing a Business
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This variable-credit course is about effectively scaling a business. Because growth is an imperative for many organizations, it is crucial to understand the economic fundamentals underpinning profitable growth. This course connects frameworks from economics to the experiences of firms attempting growth initiatives to illustrate why some businesses can scale successfully while others struggle.

title: Roadside MBA: The Economics of Growing a Business
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This two-credit course is about effectively scaling a business. Because growth is an imperative for many organizations, it is crucial to understand the economic fundamentals underpinning profitable growth. This course connects frameworks from economics to the experiences of firms attempting growth initiatives to illustrate why some businesses can scale successfully while others struggle. Recommended Prerequisites: (BUS 2010 OR QAMO 2010 OR BUS 2011 OR QAMO 2011) AND STRAT 3700.

college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: Modeling and control of manipulation and mobile robots are studied. Kinematics, interaction forces, and motion control for purposes of manipulation and mobility will be examined. Projects provide hands-on experience.

college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.

title: Rock Climbing IV
description: The basic procedures involved with the activity of rock climbing will be explained, demonstrated, and practiced during this course. All skills including those associated with lead climbing will be explored, taught and managed in a single pitch setting. "Leave No Trace" skills, and associated safety skills will be taught and applied throughout the course. Students will also explore the issues and guidelines related to the management and usage of public lands as they relate to recreational use.

title: Rock Mechanics Applications
description: Slope Stability; Elastic design of underground excavations in rock, support systems--bolting, steel sets, concrete liners, stope fill, mine subsidence.

title: Rock Rescue I - Bottom Site Management
description: The basic procedures involved with the activity of vertical self rescue in a bottom managed situation will be explained, demonstrated and practiced during this course. Leave No Trace skills, and associated safety skills including proper equipment selection and use will also be covered. Additionally, students will demonstrate an increased understanding of issues and guidelines.

title: Rock Rescue II - Top Site Management
description: The basic procedures involved with the activity of vertical self rescue in a top managed situation will be explained, demonstrated, and practiced during this course. Leave No Trace skills and associated safety skills including proper equipment selection and use will be covered. Additionally, students will demonstrate an increased understanding of issues and guidelines related to the management and usage of administered public lands, such as those used in this class as they relate to vertical self rescue and other uses.

title: Rock Rescue III - Top Site Management
description: The advanced procedures involved with the activity of vertical self rescue in a top managed situation will be explained, demonstrated, and practiced during this course. Leave No Trace skills, and associated safety skills including proper equipment selection and use will also be covered. Additionally, students will demonstrate an increased understanding of issues and guidelines related to the management and usage of administered public lands, such as those used in this class as they relate to vertical self rescue and other uses.

title: Rocks and Minerals
description: Nontechnical examination of the physics and chemistry of rock-forming minerals occurrence and origins of major rock types. Identification and classification of common minerals and rocks. Two lectures and one lab weekly.

title: Role of Law in Society
description: The purpose of this course is to gain a basic understanding of how the American legal system works and its relationship to American society. The course will focus on the evolution of our modern legal system, current intellectual movements, the interplay between law and social changes, and the main concerns and issues in the profession and practice of law.

title: Role of the Nurse Practitioner
description: Required for Doctor of Nursing Nurse Practitioner students to investigate the wide range of current and emerging advanced practice roles while valuing the contributions of other health professionals in complex healthcare environments.

title: Role Transitions
description: This course emphasizes the importance of understanding nursing roles, legal and ethical factors, and the impact of technology on patient care. Learning about health promotion, safety, quality initiatives, and the influence of social determinants is crucial for providing equitable, effective care. Mastering these concepts supports baccalaureate-prepared nurses in navigating complex healthcare environments, promotes continuous professional growth, and enhances patient outcomes, ensuring the delivery of high-quality, compassionate care

title: Roles and Values
description: Study of the theoretical basis and analytical processes fundamental to the practice of professional nursing, including health, nursing praxis, professionalism, caring, and personhood. Content will be examined from a nursing perspective and in the context of ethical and legal issues, critical thinking, and social criticism.

title: Roman Britain
description: This course will examine the History of Roman Britain from its Prehistory and Iron Age Celtic background, through the invasions of Julius Caesar, the Roman Conquest, and the history of Britain down to the coming of the Saxons. The course will discuss the development of Romano-British society, culture and economy; the Romanization of the providence and its place in the Roman Empire down to the collapse of the Roman authority; and through Dark age Britain to the beginning of the Anglo Saxon Kingdoms.

title: Roman Empire
description: Topics covering Roman historical development from fall of the Republic to the collapse of the western provinces of the Roman Empire.

title: Roman Republic
description: Topics covering Roman historical development from prehistory down to the assassination of Caesar.

title: Romance Philology
description: Main linguistic transformations in Vulgar Latin and Romance languages.

title: Romantic Music
description: In-depth discussion of issues related to 19th-century music, including repertoire, aesthetics, compositional techniques, and social context.

title: Romantic Music Grad
description: In-depth discussion of issues related to 19th-century music, including repertoire, aesthetics, compositional techniques, and social context.

title: Romanticism
description: Historical, philosophical, and cultural background of epoch (1798 to 1835). Theoretical, lyric, and prose texts from early and late Romanticism.

title: Romanticism and Realism
description: XIX Century Spanish literature from Romanticism to the end of the century. Movements and genres.

title: Rudiments of Music
description: To be offered only to music majors for the purpose of remediation. Non-majors should consult MUSC 1460 - Intro to Music Theory.

title: Rugby
description: This course involves skill development and curriculum relative to the game of Rugby.

title: Rural and Underserved Medicine: Mentored Community-Oriented Health Improvement Project
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: UUSOM students pursuing a Graduate Certificate in Rural and Underserved Medicine (GCRUM) must complete a Community-Oriented Health Improvement (COHI) Capstone Project during a 3rd or 4th year elective to earn the Graduate Certificate. This mentored 4-credit elective, along with the rural, underserved and community health prerequisite courses (MD ID 6550, 6555, 6660, and 6665), will provide the foundational principals and experiential support needed to successful complete this capstone. With assistance from the Course Directors, students will identify a mentor with knowledge and experience in community health collaboration and quality improvement efforts. Identifying a mentor can begin as early as MS1 – the sooner this process begins, the greater the opportunity to consider the many options available across the University and within the community. Faculty leads in rural and underserved medicine will assist students in identifying a COHI-project mentor, who may be a faculty member from any number of Schools or Colleges across UU (School of Medicine, School of Dentistry, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy, College of Health, College of Social Work, College of Education), or a partner in community health outside UU (ie Utah Department of Health, Utah Department of Human Services, Utah Department of Workforce Services).

college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine

title: Rural Psychiatric Mental Health Nursing
description: Web course. This course is designed as an overview of major mental disorders as they are treated in a rural community. Student will become familiar with protocols appropriate for evaluation, diagnosis, treatment and referral when in this unique setting.

title: Russia and Asia
description: Examines Russia and/or the Soviet Union in the context of Asia. Topic will vary. Readings and Discussion in English.

title: Russia under the Czars
description: An exploration of Russian consciousness in the Czarist period as exemplified in various literary, philosophical, and historical texts, as well as film. Of particular focus will be Russia’s imperial expansion into Siberia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia.

title: Russian Abroad
description: This course is for students who participate on a University of Utah Study Abroad Program in Russia. Students will spend five weeks studying intensive Russian language and exploring issues in contemporary Russian culture.

title: Russian Conversation
description: This course provides students the opportunity to improve their skills in speaking and listening, to expand their cultural awareness, and to increase their self confidence in the language. Designed to be taken with RUSS 1020, 2010,  or 2020, but open to any student not enrolled at the 3000/4000 level. No written work. Credit/Non-credit grading.

title: Russian Culture
description: Introduction to contemporary Russian culture. Readings and discussion in Russian.

title: Russian Fairy Tales
description: This course introduces students to Russian folklore through the genre of fairy tales (from oral tales to literary fairy tales and film versions) in their aesthetic, historical, social, and psychological contexts, so as to acquaint them with structures of thought underpinning modes of Russian culture and behavior. Readings and discussion in English.

title: Russian Foreign Policy
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: An examination of the sources, motivations, and strategies of Russian foreign policy with emphasis on Russian relations with the near abroad, Europe, the United States, China, and the former Communist states of East Europe.

title: Russian Morphology
description: This course presents an overview of inflectional and derivational morphology in Contemporary Standard Russian. This course is taught in English.

title: Russian Morphology
description: This course presents an overview of inflectional and derivational morphology in Contemporary Standard Russian. This course is taught in English.

title: Russian Phonetics and Phonology
description: This course presents the phonetic and phonological systems of Contemporary Standard Russian with an emphasis on both theoretical understanding and practical application of the course content. This course is taught in English.

title: Russian Phonetics and Phonology
description: This course presents the phonetic and phonological systems of Contemporary Standard Russian with an emphasis on both theoretical understanding and practical application of the course content. This course is taught in English.

title: Russian/Post-Soviet Politics
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: The Soviet political system, 1917-1991 and transformations leading to the break-up of the USSR in 1991; emerging forms of government and politics in Russia.

title: RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE)
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: During this course, medical students will travel to a rural/underserved location in the Intermountain West to complete hands-on learning with providers of different specialties. As part of this 4-week rotation, students will meet their 2-credit hour requirement in health system science by gathering community specific data & completing community interviews to identify a pressing health concern in their community. Through the knowledge learned from these experiences, medical students will create & disseminate a community deliverable/intervention that addresses the public health concern they identified. At the completion of the experience, they will develop a poster presentation that reflects their community data & intervention that will be presented in the fall during a research symposium.

title: RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE)
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE) is an opportunity for medical students to gain hands-on clinical learning for a longer period of time than medical students typically get during their first and second years of medical school. During this course, medical students will travel to a rural and/or underserved location in Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, or Montana to complete hands-on learning with providers of different specialties. Students will also participate in volunteer opportunities within the community. Additionally, they will be required to gather community specific data (community assets, demographics, epidemiology) and complete community interviews to identify a pressing health concern in their community. Through the knowledge learned from these experiences, medical students will create and disseminate a community deliverable/intervention that addresses the public health concern they identified. At the completion of the experience, they will develop a poster presentation that reflects their community data and intervention that will be presented later in the fall during a research symposium. Various assignments will be completed (described below) to draw deeper into the students’ experience as a health professional in rural and/or underserved communities and to help them develop their community deliverable/intervention. Community deliverable topics will come out of a community assessment and may focus on any number of public health topics, including: physical health (e.g. diabetes), behavioral health (e.g. substance use disorders), social determinants of health (e.g. income level), and emerging issues (vaccination resistance). 1 Summary of Course Components: 1. Complete hands-on clinical learning 2. Volunteer in the community 3. Investigate and create a community deliverable, which the student will implement/propose to the community 4. Once the CEE experience is completed, the student will reflect on their experience and create a poster presentation to summarize their intervention in the community *(See Course Format and Schedule for More Detailed Information on Course Components) Much of our inspiration for the CEE Program is from University of Washington’s Rural/Underserved Opportunities Program (RUOP). RUOP leadership was instrumental in sharing their course curriculum to help shape the CEE experience at the University of Utah School of Medicine. 1

title: RUUTE Community Preceptorship
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: The RUUTE Community Preceptorship elective will allow medical students to explore medical practice in rural communities across Utah, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. Students will be exposed to the diverse training pathways that lend themselves to rural practice by having the opportunity to rotate with one or many preceptors including Family Medicine, Med-Peds, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, OB/GYN, Psychiatry, Neurology, Surgery and/or Emergency Medicine across the community. Other specialties will be considered on a case by case basis. Students will be exposed to a diverse range of healthcare delivery systems, observing how these systems serve clinicians, patients and communities as a whole. This course can be taken concurrently with RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE). Students must enroll in both courses individually.

title: Sacred Space in the Near East
college: SB - Coll of Soc & Behavioral Sci
description: Meets with ANTH 6136. This course is designed to demonstrate how sacred space in the Near East manifested itself, i.e., how it was chosen and used, how it was differentiated from profane areas, and how viable it was for adaptation to socio-political and socio-religious changes. Due to the massive amount of available data on sacral places from Anatolia, Egypt, Iran, Mesopotamia, and Syria-Palestine, only selected examples of temples and/or sanctuaries and /or funerary sacred enclosures will be discussed within an appropriate cultural context.

title: Safety Issues in Transportation
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: Meets with CVEEN 6520.  Safety as it relates to geometrical design, roadside safety, safety management systems, safety analysis, traffic control devices, work zone safety, risk management, education and enforcement, railroad safety.

title: Safety Issues in Transportation
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: Meets CVEEN 5840.  Safety as it relates to geometrical design, roadside safety, safety management systems, safety analysis, traffic control devices, work zone safety, risk management, education and enforcement, railroad safety.

title: Sailing - Introduction to Basic Keelboat
description: Learn the fundamentals of sailing, including theory, safety, points of sail, primary first aid in a marine environment, basic knots, basic boat maintenance, and rigging. Students will learn and act at each of the positions to crew and sail a vessel (bowman, navigator, cockpit crew, helmsman, and captain.) Spend four days at the Great Salt Lake sailing several different sailboats. sailboats are provided. American Sailing Association (ASA) 101 certification is available. Course includes two classroom sessions and four weekend sailing sessions.

title: Sales Management Decisions
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: Junior standing. Operations and decisions associated with managing a sales effort; organizing, training, and managing the sales force; sales forecasting; sales analysis and allocation of sales effort; pricing policies. Some sections taught as writing emphasis; see Writing Program in this section of the catalog for explanation.

title: Sales Technology, Analytics, and Operations
college: BU - David Eccles Sch of Business
description: This course provides an in-depth introduction to the technology tools used by professional salespeople as they take prospects along the journey from target market to committed loyal customer. Topics include targeting tools, content delivery, data enrichment, lead generation, lead tracking and nurturing, sales funnel management, customer relationship management, social media tools, and spend optimization. Students will learn how to use technologies to analyze new forms of customer data, enhance their ability to forecast customer behavior, and develop and execute effective monetization strategies.

title: Salt Lake City Workshop
description: The Salt Lake City Workshop brings together students with community partners to envision best possibilities for our city and work toward realizing them. To do this, students will learn about place-making community-building, public scholarship, and urban leadership. Students will focus these efforts on developing a selected project for Salt Lake City.

title: Salt Lake County Parks and Recreation
description: This course offers a variety of fitness classes that students may take part in. Classes offered vary by location, and generally include the following: Yoga, Zumba, Cycling, Water Aerobics, Circuit Training, Body Pump, TRX, Lebarre, and Core. Any additional classes that fall under the location’s Group Fitness Classes included in their community membership are also available for students.  **Fitness classes offered for a separate rate (generally listed separately from the Group Fitness Classes and marked with a “*” in the schedule) are not available for students.   **Pilates, Kickboxing, and Boot Camp are also unavailable for students.

title: SAS Lab III
description: For students who wish to participate only in the Lab component of MATH 3090.

title: Scale Development
description: How to develop measurement instruments for research use (thesis and dissertations) when no acceptable published tests exist. Student projects are emphasized. Students enrolled in 7320 will be held to a higher standard and may be assigned additional work.

title: Scale Development
description: How to develop measurement instruments for research use (thesis and dissertations) when no acceptable published tests exist. Student projects are emphasized. Students enrolled in 7320 will be held to a higher standard and may be assigned additional work.

title: Scandinavian Architecture
description: Survey of historical and contemporary architecture and design of Scandinavia.

title: Scandinavian Film & Literature
description: This course explores film adaptations of select Scandinavian novels, short stories, poems, and plays. We will examine strategies of bringing written texts to the screen, and we will study key works of the cinemas and belles-lettres of Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Finland.

title: Scanning Electron Microscopy
college: EN - J & M Price College of Eng.
description: Review of vacuum technology, electron sources and electron optics. Components of the electron microscope, their principles of operation and failure modes. Aspects of image quality and their optimization. Review of atomic physics and characteristics x-ray emission. Principles and operation of instrumentation for Elemental Determination by Analysis of X-rays. Generation and calibration of standards.

title: Scanning Electron Microscopy
description: The SEM: capabilities, advantages and limitations. Electron sources, electron optics and detectors. Components of the electron microscope, their principles of operation and failure modes. Image quality, optimization and interpretation. Decision tree and analytical strategies for microscopy. Review of atomic physics and characteristic x-ray emission. Principles and operation of instrumentation for elemental analysis by Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy, discussion of pitfalls and strategies. Low vacuum, ESEM and Focused Ion Beam. Lectures are based on lab exercises. Recommended Prerequisites: PHYS 2220 & CHEM 1210 OR Instructor Consent.

title: Scene Design I
description: For Theatre Majors and Minors. Students explore modern stage design through lectures and assigned projects that develop drawing, sketching, and model building techniques.

title: Scene Design II
description: For Theatre Majors and Minors. An advanced design studio course emphasizing the development of the design process through period research, sketching, and script analysis.

title: Scene Painting
description: For Theatre Majors and Non-Majors. This is a hands-on studio course. Students will learn basic and intermediate scenic artist painting techniques that are used for both stage and film scenic production. Techniques include: texturing, marbling, wood graining, faux painting, and drop painting.

title: Scenic Drafting
description: Drafting techniques for designers and  technicians.

title: Scenography
description: For Theatre Majors and Minors. Theatre Core Requirement. An introduction to the art of scenography, including the ways in which theatre artists communicate visually, and the way audiences read information in a theatrical design. This course has a lab component.

title: Scenography Lab
description: Theatre core requirement for Theatre Majors and Minors. This is a lab experience in the areas of scenic, lighting, sound, properties, and technical direction. Students will learn basic terminology, tools, and design skills for scenography as an integral part of the storytelling and performance process.

title: Scenography Lecture
description: For Theatre Majors and Minors. An introduction to the art of scenography--a performance-art design practice that focuses on visual elements to promote audience reception and engagement in storytelling. Scenographers study the text, develop ideas with a director, address performers' needs, and analyze how audiences read these elements, in order to create the imaginative and appropriate environments of set, properties, costumes, lighting, and sound.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar I
description: The purpose of this credit/no-credit seminar is to actively engage the graduate student in exploration of professional roles and exposure to a wide range of peer-reviewed articles relevant to their research interests. Students will participate in regular discussion and critiques at journal clubs. Articles will be connected to theoretical frameworks or social determinants of health as well as student research interests.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar II
description: The purpose of this credit/no-credit seminar is to actively engage the graduate student in exploration of research design thinking/approaches and integration of theory and data in research. Through journal clubs, students will be exposed to a wide range of peer-reviewed articles which include diverse designs and approaches relevant to their research interests. Articles will be connected to theoretical frameworks or social determinants of health as well as student research interest.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar III
description: This seminar provides a collaborative environment for students to present and discuss their ongoing research in progress, including abstracts, manuscripts and grant proposals. Emphasizing critical feedback and peer engagement, the course fosters a culture of scholarly exchange and iterative improvement. Students will take turns presenting their work-in-progress, receiving constructive critique, and refining their methodologies, theoretical frameworks, and analyses based on this feedback. Each session will include discussions on research design, data collection techniques, ethical considerations, and effective communication of findings. Throughout the semester, students will develop essential skills in public speaking, scholarly writing, and critical thinking.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar IV
description: In this student-driven integration seminar, participants take the lead in identifying and analyzing current journal articles and exploring professional standards with an emphasis on data collection, management, and analysis. Through peer-led discussions and projects, as well as journal club sessions, students will enhance their research skills and critically evaluate data collection, management, and analytic methods.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar V
description: This seminar course highlights ethical leadership, advanced research methodologies and implementation science. Through case studies, collaborative projects, and presentations, students will refine their leadership skills while developing sophisticated research strategies to advance nursing science and contribute to policy development and healthcare innovation. Students will prepare for their comprehensive exam through group discussion, mock sessions and presentations.

title: Scholarly Integration Seminar VI
description: This seminar focuses on the principles and practices of effectively disseminating research through abstracts, manuscripts, and funding proposals. In a collaborative learning environment, students will critically analyze scholarly communication and learn to write for and present to diverse audiences. Participants will refine their skills in crafting compelling abstracts for conferences, structuring manuscripts for peer-reviewed journals, and designing persuasive grant proposals. The course emphasizes the specific requirements of various publication and funding venues, aligning research questions and approaches with funding and policy priorities, and the ethical considerations in dissemination.

title: Scholarly Research Project
description: Graduate independent study resulting in production of a research paper (15-20 pages) in support of the chosen field of study and as part of preparation for the graduate thesis.

title: Scholarly Writing
description: This graduate level course serves as an overview of a variety of approaches to creating and maintaining a scholarly writing practice.

title: Scholarly Writing and the Critical Review of Academic Literature
description: This course focuses on the use of the written word to advance the mission of social work as well as individual academic careers. It is designed to give students an introduction to the political economy of academic discourse from the political dynamics that influence editorial decision-making to the economic considerations that determine the fate (and content) of journals. We will explore the craft of scholarly writing. Students will also read and critique published articles on a wide range of topics, conduct regular peer reviews of work in progress, and prepare a critical review of the literature in their chosen fields.

title: Scholarly Writing and the Critical Review of Academic Literature II
description: This course introduces students to the processes involved in submitting and reviewing journal articles. It introduces the political economy of academic discourse, addressing dynamics that influence editorial decision-making and economic considerations that can determine the fate (and content of journals). We will discuss the workings of copyrights and the relationship between authors and publishers. Students will review drafts of articles in their chosen fields and conduct peer reviews of their work-in-progress. (1) Academic Discourse: students will participate in the review of a manuscript submitted for publication (under the instructor’s supervision (2) Writing Practice: Continue work on publishable manuscript with the goal of completing a first draft. (3) Mechanics and Craft: Writing as Thinking, developing a unique (professional) voice; (standing out from the crowd). Students will complete a first draft of a publishable manuscript. This document will be workshopped in class. Evaluation will be based on: manuscript, peer feedback, and journal review.

title: Scholarly Writing and the Critical Review of Academic Literature III
description: This semester students will consolidate the lessons learned previously and will complete revision of their manuscript, which will be submitted for publication. We will discuss how to choose a journal, respond to revise and resubmit decisions and interact with editors. They may also work on their research (and teaching?) statements in preparation for the job search. The work prepared for this class may link with the students’ work for their qualifying examinations. (1) Academic Discourse: students will submit a manuscript for publication and discuss the distinct aspects involved in drafting a complex analytic paper (2) Writing Practice: Close reading. Students will complete and submit their manuscripts, which will be workshopped in class. Evaluation will be based on successful completion of research (& teaching?) statements, manuscript, peer reviews.

title: Scholarly Writing Workshop
description: This course focuses on the use of the written word to advance the mission of social work as well as individual academic careers. It is designed to give students an introduction to the political economy of academic discourse from the political dynamics that influence editorial decision-making to the economic considerations that determine the fate (and content) of journals. We will explore the craft of scholarly writing. Students will also read and critique published articles on a wide range of topics, conduct regular peer reviews of work in progress, and prepare a critical review of the literature in their chosen fields

title: Scholarship in Sports Medicine
description: This is a directed project course with a member of the Athletic Training staff or faculty. This could include research, clinical experiences, internships, or other such projects. In general, this course is for students with an advanced understanding of the athletic training field and sports medicine.

title: Scholarship Practices for the Academic Professional
description: This course covers the professional practices of scholarship in communication, including theses, research proposals, consulting reports, book prospecti, convention presentations and journal articles in traditional and new media forms.

title: School and Society
description: Explores the social and institutional context of schooling. Addresses history of education; anthropology and sociology of education; and philosophy of education. Focuses on issues of diversity, including policy, curriculum, pedagogy and relationships.

title: School Change & Reform
description: Examines specific reform efforts, explores promising practices, and requires participation in a change project.

title: School Psychology Practicum: Clinic
description: Supervised experience in psychological services in schools, hospitals, and clinic settings. Assessment, intervention and consultation emphasized.

title: School Psychology Practicum: Field
description: Supervised field experiences in psychological services. Students are placed in schools and other settings. Assessment and intervention emphasized.

title: School Psychology Seminar: Autism
description: Seminar is related to grant for the US Dept. of Education to prepare school psychologists to work with students who have autism and other related disabilities.

title: School Psychology Seminar: Evidence Based Practice
description: This seminar is proposed in conjunction with a US Office of Education Grant: Personnel Preparation Grant. The seminar investigates what constitutes evidence based practice in the treatment of children and adolescents with psychological/behavioral disorders.

title: School Psychology Seminar: Positive Behavior
description: This seminar is proposed in conjunction with a US Office of Education: Personnel Preparation Grant. The seminar investigates Positive Behavior Support, Response to Intervention, and conducting Functional Behavior Assessments in school settings for children and adolescents with psychological disorders.

title: School Psychology Seminar: Preparing School Faculty
description: Seminar is related to grant for the US Dept of Education to prepare future school psychology faculty to teach and conduct research in the area of autism and other related disabilities.

title: School Psychology-Research Practicum
description: This course sequence will provide school psychology students with an introductory experience in research relevant to the theory and practice of school psychology. Students will be able to develop and enhance research related conceptualization, design, analysis, and writing skills necessary to apply research in the schools and provide a foundational experience for dissertation level research.

title: School Social Work Field Practicum - Generalist
description: Field Practicum applies theoretical knowledge and models of social work to agency practice with diverse populations at risk. Students apply generalist perspective to develop ethically competent practice in micro, mezzo, and macro areas of social work under the supervision of an approved clinical instructor. Students gain skills in maintaining working relationships, developing multi-dimensional assessment, utilizing a lifespan perspective, differentially applying intervention strategies taking into account the unique attributes of each client system, and conducting appropriate evaluations of practice interventions. Ethics, knowledge, values, and skills.

title: School Social Work Field Practicum - Generalist
description: Field Practicum applies theoretical knowledge and models of social work to agency practice with diverse populations at risk. Students apply generalist perspective to develop ethically competent practice in micro, mezzo, and macro areas of social work under the supervision of an approved clinical instructor. Students gain skills in maintaining working relationships, developing multi-dimensional assessment, utilizing a lifespan perspective, differentially applying intervention strategies taking into account the unique attributes of each client system, and conducting appropriate evaluations of practice interventions. Ethics, knowledge, values, and skills.

title: School Social Work Field Practicum - Specialist
description: Students apply advanced roles, models, and theories of social work within an agency placement that supports their specialist year domain of study. Under the supervision of an approved clinical instructor, students build upon the generalist perspective and increase their skills in ethical, culturally-competent, multi-modal social work practice.

title: School Social Work Field Practicum - Specialist
description: Students apply advanced roles, models, and theories of social work within an agency placement that supports their second-year domain of study. Under the supervision of an approved clinical instructor, students build upon the generalist perspective and increase their skills in ethical, culturally-competent, multi-modal social work practice.

title: School Social Work Macro Skills
description: This course offers an orientation to social work practice in schools. Students will become familiar with traditional and changing social work roles and practices in schools as well as with larger systemic trend, which impact school settings and school-based social work.

title: School Social Work Micro Skills
description: This course focuses on the knowledge, micro skills and values appropriate for social work practice within the school setting. Special attention is given to working with students, teachers, parents and administrators as well as collaborating with the community. Emphasis is placed on the tasks of social assessment for educational and behavioral planning, the formulation of goals and objectives to meet students and families' behavioral health and physical needs; and accessing school resources and external referrals. Teaching curriculum will include evidence-based practices for behavioral interventions, problem solving strategies, brief and group treatment social skills treatment and utilizing school data to link with age appropriate interventions.

title: School, Home, and Community Partnerships
description: Meets with SP ED 5010.  Theories, models, and strategies of collaborative partnerships to meet the needs of students with disabilities in home, school, and community settings.  Additional assignments required for graduate credit.

title: School, Work and State
description: Basic principals and concepts that underlie Marxist, neo-Marxist, Post-structuralist, and other radical approaches to the study of education. Students enrolled in ECS 7615 will be held to a higher standard of performance and may be assigned additional work.

title: School, Work, and the State
description: Basic principles and concepts that underlie Marxist, neo-Marxist, Post-structuralist, and other radical approaches to the study of education. Students enrolled in ECS 7615 will be held to a higher standard of performance and may be assigned additional work.

title: School-wide Positive Behavior Support
description: This course will provide instruction on the three-tiered model of school-wide positive behavior support. Students will learn how to develop and evaluate interventions at the primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of behavior support.

title: Schools and Inequality
description: Combines ethnographic studies of students' resistance to schooling with curriculum research intended to explain the educational practices of U.S. schools. Focuses on the influence of divisions of class, race, and gender.

title: Schoolwide Support, Consultation, and Interagency Collaboration
description: As a function of participating in this course, students will develop skills associated with team facilitation and leadership, behavioral consultation, multi-agency collaboranion and community-based planning.

title: Science & Storytelling II
description: Continuation of HONOR 2600, Science & Storytelling Learning Community. How do we communicate through stories about our sensory experiences of the world? Through this course, students discover how the relationship between art and science manifests itself in individuals, in disciplines and in society. In addition, we'll explore questions at the interface between science and art and we'll consider the ways in which art and science offer us models of knowledge through which we see and understand the world. We'll learn about sensory systems and perception and how science and art help us understand how these systems work. We will look at the ways that the institution of knowledge, such as museums and schools, shape our understanding of the categories 'art' and 'science'.

title: Science ACCESS Program
description: The summer PHYCS 1430 is taken by the ACCESS cohort after their selection as ACCESS Scholarship winners.  This integrated science program focuses on weekly laboratory experiments in biology, physics, and chemistry. The glue connecting these experimental selections is collection of mathematical techniques that are taught during the course, and then applied to the experiments which are performed. Taught by faculty from all the departments of the College of Science. An objective of this program is to assist each ACCESS student in making an informed decision about the area of science that will most interest her. During the spring semester each ACCESS student is placed in a research lab somewhere on campus based on her expressed preference, which this summer general education course helped clarify.

title: Science and Culture in Japan
description: The aim of this course is to explore the role of science in Japan. In particular, the course will study three periods: the Ritsuryo system and the introduction of Chinese intellectual culture, the early modern Edo period and engagement with European science, and the Meiji period adoption of European science. The course will be taught in English and readings will be in English.

title: Science and Culture in the Islamicate World
description: This course introduces students the role and development of science in the Islamicate world. In particular, it examines the development of the rational sciences, their relationship to the revealed (religious) sciences, and how they flourished. The period of study will explore the early Islamicate world, medieval Islam, the early modern world, and modern engagement with science such as with Salama Musa and Muhammad Abduh.

title: Science and Pedagogy
description: This course created by the Honors Think Tank on Astronomy will familiarize future students with the fundamentals of astronomy and equip them with the skills necessary to educate others. Students in the course will master teaching kits used by the Clark Planetarium and will take their new knowledge to Salt Lake City's elementary schools. Students in the course will work to eradicate misconceptions about astronomy while increasing their own scientific knowledge and serving their communities.

title: Science and Risk Communication
description: Advanced study of science and risk communication theories relevant to public opinion formation and dynamics. Science and risk communication are central to understanding STEM issues that have significant ethical, legal, and social implications at the intersection of media and politics.

title: Science and Society
description: SCI 2020 is a project-based course. In this course, students will learn how science and society are integrated through scientific inquiries, case studies involving ethical dilemmas, group discussions and a community-engaged project. Students will also interact with inspirational faculty, learn about research opportunities, and participate in field trips. Students will communicate their learning through writing, discussion, and oral and poster presentations. This course is intended to provide context for science majors as they progress through future coursework and scientific careers, and serve as a foundation for non-science majors to become part of a scientifically literate society.

title: Science and Society
description: Examines the impact of both science on society and of society on science. It will discuss the way in which science is a social enterprise and is affected by social demands. Case studies for studying the intersection of science and society will be drawn from such areas as the history of physics, the development of genetics, the measurement of human intelligence.

title: Science and Storytelling
description: How do vision, hearing, taste, smell and touch work? How do we communicate through storied about our sensory experiences of the world? Through this course, students discover how the relationship between art and science manifests itself in individuals, in disciplines and in society. In addition, we'll explore questions at the interface between science and art and we'll consider the ways in which art and science offer us models of knowledge through which we see and understand the world. We'll learn about sensory systems and perception and how science and art help us understand how these system work. We will look at the ways that the institutions of knowledge, such as museums and schools, shape our understanding of the categories 'art' and 'science.'

title: Science Communication and Mentoring Skill for the Next Generation
description: The ability to communicate effectively to peers, professionals and the public is critical to being successful in any scientific field. Science addresses questions that are integral to some of today's most pressing political and social issues including health care, environmental quality, technology and education. Therefore, scientists must be able to place their work in a context that is relevant and accessible to a broad audience. This course is designed to teach students how to communicate complex interdisciplinary scientific concepts through written and oral mediums and to prepare them to communicate successfully with peers, researchers, faculty, students, and future employers. The course consists of a 2-hour class session and a 3-hour weekly communication and teaching lab in a K-12 school.

title: Science Communication, Special Topics
description: Course explores current topics in science communication and reflects current events and faculty expertise. May be taken two times for credit.

title: Science Education Outreach Methods and Practice
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: This course is a unique opportunity for highly-motivated undergraduate and graduate students to learn about outreach programs and actively participate in a primary and secondary Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) education program that targets children with limited opportunities. Weekly lectures will focus on how to identify needs of a community and creation of an outreach program to fulfill that need. A special emphasis will be placed on developing skills to communicate with the public. In addition to weekly lectures, students will spend a minimum of 40 hours/semester assisting with classroom, afterschool, and outreach STEM-related activities. There is a mandatory course orientation on the Thursday before classes begin from 1:00pm-5:00pm. Failure to attend orientation may result in being dropped from the course. Please check Canvas and Umail frequently for further updates.

title: Science Fiction
description: Introduction to writing and film that include aliens, advanced technology, androids, space travel, time travel, and the like.

title: Science in a Changing World
description: Explore the challenges associated with using a growing body of scientific knowledge to inform decisions pertaining to our understanding and use of energy. The curriculum in this “STEAM” (STEM with integration of arts and humanities) based course affords students with an opportunity to learn about contemporary research and the interplay between science, engineering, and society. Students engage in activities that complement instruction, foster a peer and campus community, and support academic success throughout their time at the U.

title: Science Methods
description: Introduction to methods of teaching inquiry-based science. Emphasis is placed on developing the ability to implement the process of scientific inquiry in the classroom. This course focuses on understanding the nature of science, lesson planning, managing an inquiry-based classroom, student assessment, and methods of inclusive science teaching for diverse student populations. Community/School field hours are expected to be completed as part of this class.

title: Science Methods
description: Introduction to methods of teaching inquiry-based science. Emphasis is placed on developing the ability to implement the process of scientific inquiry in the classroom. This course focuses on understanding the nature of science, lesson planning, managing an inquiry-based classroom, student assessment, and methods of inclusive science teaching for diverse student populations. Community/School field hours are expected to be completed as part of this class.

title: Science of Endodontics
description: Introduction to clinical science of the diseased tooth requiring endodontic therapy. Anatomy of the dental pulp chamber and root canal structures will be reviewed. The dentin/pulp complex will be studied and considered in relation to treatment options.

title: Science of Endodontics II - Applications
description: Science and application of endodontic procedures (II).

title: Science of Endurance Training
description: This course will challenge students to build up their understanding of exercise physiology for the purpose of better understanding the training and development of endurance sport performance. In addition to exploring general training adaptation concepts and principles, the biological basis of specific training adaptations essential to endurance performance will be examined. Strategies for optimizing function of the physiological and metabolic systems fundamental to endurance sport performance will also be examined.

title: Science of Medicine
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Continuation of first year course with focus on evidence based medicine and information management.

title: Science of Medicine
college: MD - S. F. E. School of Medicine
description: Interdisciplinary course that introduces evidence based medicine and information management using the tools of medical investigation and data analysis, including the principles of study design, statistical inference, data interpretation, and computer-assisted information gathering.

title: Science of Power Training
description: This courses will examine the biological basis of developing strength and power. The mechanism of neuromuscular, endocrine, connective, skeletal, and cardiovascular tissue adaptation to strength and power training will also be explored. The importance of appropriate nutrient required to fuel training will also be integrated throughout the course. Hands-on experience will focus on developing strength and power training programs for active individuals in addition to learning advanced training techniques and safety concerns that accompany them.

title: Science on Stage
description: In this course, we bring together the human experience of the scientist with its public perception as embodied in theatre. After all, what is more dramatic than the excitement (and terror) of discovery, that moment when the earth seems to shift beneath one's feet and everything appears change? Playwrights have seen an explosion of new plays about science and scientists. Science on Stage explores the range of science plays now available, with a particular interest in understanding how they reflect the public understanding of science, as well as understanding the science and theatre history that informs the play' content and form. Students will read plays on a variety of scientific, cultural, and theatrical terms. Throughout the semester, students will collaborate in interdisciplinary teams to discuss and synthesize course material in the conception of an original live performance event about science.

title: Science Research Initiative Undergraduate Research
description: This course offers undergraduate students the opportunity to deeply engage in the scientific process while gaining essential skills, including observation, written and oral communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving, in a collaborative environment. Students will develop these skills through cohort-based research experiences (Research Streams) as part of the Science Research Initiative. Each research Stream will be supervised by a faculty mentor from the College of Science. Students will be working on an independent project- the degree to which the student conceptualizes and designs that project is largely up to the mentor. The specific laboratory skills and disciplinary knowledge learned while carrying out research will vary depending on the focus of the research project. In addition to acquiring research Stream specific disciplinary expertise, participation will generally develop skills for reviewing scientific literature, data collection and data analyses, and scientific communication.

title: Science Student Success
description: A student success course with presentations from campus partners, college faculty, and peer mentors. This series focuses on connecting students to resources for a successful undergraduate career in science, including navigating the choices they will make as majors as well as opportunities for internships, research and outreach.

title: Science Teaching Methods (Elem)
description: One week workshop intended for practicing elementary teachers. This course will focus on the physical science elements of the Utah State Core Curriculum in elementary grades. The course is designed as an intensive one-week summer workshop. In particular, the targeted areas addressed will be those specific items in physical science taught in Utah's public schools as required by the core curriculum document. In addition, emphasis will also be placed on the prefatory document in the core curriculum entitled "Intended Learning Outcomes" in terms of the development of course materials and how they are to be used by the participants in the course in their own classrooms. An additional focus of the course will be creative problem solving in which course participants will learn how to couch numerous science lessons as problem solving opportunities for their students. Course structure is essentially lab oriented occasionally punctuated with short lectures, participant presentations, problem-solving sessions, computer-related opportunities, and interactive exchange sessions.

title: Science Teaching Methods (Elem)
description: Two week workshop intended for practicing elementary teachers. This course will focus on the physical science elements of the Utah State Core Curriculum in elementary grades. title: Science Teaching Methods (Sec)
description: Two week workshop intended for practicing secondary teachers. This course will focus on the physical science elements of the Utah State Core Curriculum as they pertain to the physical sciences in the secondary grades. The course is designed as an intensive one-week summer workshop. In particular, the targeted areas addressed will be those specific items in physical science taught in Utah's public schools as required by the core curriculum document for those grades. In addition, emphasis will also be placed on the prefatory document in the core curriculum entitled "Intended Learning Outcomes" in terms of the development of course materials and how they are to be used by the participants in the course in their own classrooms.
